 FDA Warns Not to Eat Haifa Smoked Fish Cold Smoked Sprats: Made Without Botulism Controls, and the Company Refused to Recall Them. Sold in New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Pennsylvania, Possibly Beyond. Check Your Freezer.
 By Bill Marler on October 24, 2026 
 Posted in Food Poisoning Information 
 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is  warning consumers, retailers, wholesalers, restaurants and food service customers  not to eat, sell or serve any cold smoked sprats sold by D&M Smoked Fish Inc., doing business as Haifa Smoked Fish, Inc., of Jamaica, New York. The FDA posted the advisory on October 23, 2026.
 An FDA inspection of the Jamaica facility found that the firm was producing cold smoked sprats without the food safety controls required to prevent  Clostridium botulinum  growth and toxin formation. The FDA recommended that D&M Smoked Fish recall all cold smoked sprats currently on the market.  The company declined , so the FDA issued its own public warning instead.
 The product can be identified as follows:
 Product:  All lots of cold smoked sprats sold by D&M Smoked Fish Inc. / Haifa Smoked Fish, Inc.
 Packaging:  Bulk cardboard boxes, shipped refrigerated. The product may be kept frozen for up to one year.
 Shipping label:  Boxes pictured by the FDA read “Haifa Smoked Fish, 94-15 150 St., Jamaica, N.Y. 11435” with a product label reading “C/Smoked Holland Sprats.” The pictured boxes show Lot #261, but the warning covers all lots.
 Distribution:  Retailers, restaurants, wholesalers and food service customers in Connecticut, New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania. The FDA says the product may have reached additional states.
 Because the sprats were shipped in bulk, they may have been sold at restaurants and grocery store seafood counters with or without a label. The FDA advises anyone who cannot tell whether their sprats came from Haifa Smoked Fish not to eat them and to throw them away, or to contact the place of purchase or supplier. Anyone who had the product should clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers it touched, following  FDA’s safe food handling advice . The FDA’s advisory does not report any illnesses.
 Food contaminated with botulinum toxin can look, smell and taste normal. Cold smoking does not reach temperatures that destroy  Clostridium botulinum  spores, and small whole fish like sprats are often processed with the guts in, where spores are most likely to be concentrated. That is why federal rules require cold smoked fish processors to put specific controls in place to keep the spores from growing and producing toxin. According to the FDA, those controls were missing here.
 This is not the first time Haifa sprats have drawn regulators’ attention. In March 2011, D&M Smoked Fish  recalled Cold Smoked Sprats and Haifa brand Schmaltz Herring  after New York State testing found the fish had not been properly eviscerated, a botulism risk. In 2010, the company  recalled more than 20 Haifa smoked fish products for Listeria , cold smoked sprats among them, after an FDA sample tested positive.
 Symptoms of botulism  include nausea, vomiting, fatigue or weakness, blurred or double vision, difficulty speaking or a change in voice, difficulty swallowing, dry mouth, constipation, respiratory distress and descending paralysis that starts with the face. Symptoms usually begin 12 to 36 hours after eating contaminated food but can appear within a few hours or as late as 10 days. Botulism is a medical emergency. In severe cases, people die without intensive care, and early treatment with antitoxin is critical. Anyone who ate these sprats and develops symptoms should seek medical care immediately.
